newsitem.title: USA: Americans begin voting between Clinton, Dole.
newsitem.headline: Americans begin voting between Clinton, Dole.

text.p: Americans began voting on Tuesday with President Bill Clinton relatively confident he will win a second term and Republican challenger Bob Dole hoping for an upset victory.

Polls opened at 6 a.m. EST (1100 GMT) in several eastern states and good weather was anticipated across most of the country. Voters were also choosing 34 senators, 435 members of the House of Representatives, 11 state governors and making decisions on a variety of ballot initiatives.
The campaign trail ended for both Clinton and Dole in the pre-dawn darkness to cap a final, frenzied period of travel.

Clinton was resting in a hotel in Little Rock, Arkansas, while Dole was headed to his hometown of Russell, Kansas, after a stop in Independence, Missouri, the hometown of Harry Truman, whose legendary 1948 come-from-behind victory is the standard for all underdog candidates.
"What was true for Harry Truman in 1948 will be true for Bob Dole and Jack Kemp in 1996," said the 73-year-old Dole. "The people are once again going to win this election today."

Clinton and his team, meanwhile, were buoyant. En route from South Dakota to Arkansas, he and his wife Hillary toasted their staff and the Secret Service agents who have been away from home so often because of the campaign.
"This is the greatest country in human history because we have created a system in which you are the boss," Clinton told a final rally in Sioux City, South Dakota.

Opinion surveys that unanimously forecast re-election for Democrat Clinton also suggested that grudging voters -- happy enough economically but uninspired by Clinton personally -- might check him with another Republican Congress or even deny him the majority popular support he covets.

Late polls said the Republicans seemed likely to retain control of the 100-member Senate. But the 435-seat House of Representatives was rated too close to call and Clinton's personal support hovered around the 50 percent mark in surveys where many seemed to look upon him the lesser of two evils.

Clinton, 50, hoping to become the first Democrat re-elected president since 1944, would have to sweat out the verdict until Tuesday night along with Dole, an ex-Kansas senator and Second World War infantryman pursuing "one last mission."
Waiting with them was Ross Perot, the Texas billionaire who took nearly one vote in five in a 1992 presidential bid but seemed a far weaker force this time around.

Out of 185,000 polling stations nationwide, the residents of two tiny New Hampshire communities were the first to cast ballots in the 1996 election. Shortly after midnight, Dixville Notch and Hart's Location cast 31 votes for Dole, 20 for Clinton and five for Reform Party candidate Ross Perot.

Experts were predicting a low turnout among 148 million registered voters despite massive registration and get-out-the-vote efforts around the country. Only 55.2 percent of eligible adults voted in 1992 when Clinton won the presidency. Turnout slumped to 38.8 percent in the Congressional elections of 1994 when Republicans took majority control of both chambers.
Most polls close between 7 p.m. EDT (0001 Wednesday) in some Eastern states and 11 p.m. EDT (0400 GMT) in California.
The White House result should be known by mid-evening but control of Congress may not be clear until Wednesday, if then.

At stake besides the White House and Congress were 11 of 50 state governorships, many local offices and ballot issues ranging from whether Californians wish to use marijuana as medicine to whether Floridians will safeguard the Everglades.

The vote concluded another long, exhausting and costly U.S. election cycle that began as a lofty promise of leadership into the 21st Century and ended as a brawl dominated by attacks on Clinton's character and the alleged influence of foreign cash in his campaign and his government.
These blows caused a late sag in his big polling leads and set pulses to racing among Dole partisans -- although if they fazed the confident Clinton, he never let on.

Dole, his voice reduced to a fatigued croak, barnstormed gamely through a 96-hour, 17-state campaign finale through the last night and into Election Day, dragging a punchy entourage through airports, meeting halls, diners and ice cream parlours.

"I may not keep my voice but I will keep my word," he told one crowd in Phoenix in a dig at Clinton. "I will not violate the public trust when I'm president of the United States. I've never known such arrogance in the White House."

Election eve surveys gave Clinton leads ranging from about seven points in a Reuters poll to 18 in a CBS/New York Times survey, with most in between. Clinton's support was in the 47-53 percent range, with Dole at or below 40 percent and Perot at eight or nine points.

Clinton's lead has wavered little all year and the reason was clear: he can point to a country that is prosperous, at peace and without scarring social turmoil. Unemployment is at a seven-year low of 5.2 percent, inflation is only about 3 percent, stock market indices are sky-high, the federal deficit is barely over one-third what it was when he took office and crime rates are the lowest in a decade.
Against all that, Dole's main promises -- lower taxes and a higher moral tone in the White House -- have not sold.
